Patrick
PAT-rik
proper noun (figure)
Latin Patricius — "nobleman, member of the Roman patrician class." From pater ("father"). The Patricii were the founding senatorial families of the Roman Republic; under the empire the name became a Christian given name through the Romano-British missionary to Ireland.

📖 Biblical Definition

Patrick (c. 385 — 461 AD; some sources c. 415-493), the Romano-British missionary who brought the gospel to Ireland and became the apostle of the Irish nation, is the second figure in history (after Paul the Apostle) for whom we have a substantial autobiographical account written by a single missionary describing his own work. The two short Latin works that survive in his hand — the Confessio (a defense of his ministry written in his old age) and the Epistola ad Coroticum (a public excommunication of a British Christian warlord who enslaved Patrick's converts) — show a man of disarming theological seriousness and pastoral conviction. He was born somewhere in Roman Britain to a deacon's family; captured by Irish raiders at age sixteen; enslaved for six years tending sheep in (probably) County Mayo, where his Christian faith deepened in solitude and prayer; escaped at age twenty-two and made his way back to Britain; eventually returned to Ireland as a missionary bishop (c. 432 in the traditional dating). For roughly thirty years he traveled the island, baptizing tens of thousands, ordaining clergy, planting churches, confronting druidic religion, and accepting noble women into monastic life against the conventions of the age. By his death in 461 (or 493) Christianity was the dominant religion of Ireland. His Confessio contains no shamrock-and-Trinity legend (a medieval embellishment), no snake-banishing miracle (a hagiographic invention), and very little of the green-beer culture that has subsequently attached itself to his March 17 feast day. What it contains is one of the most modest, biblically-saturated missionary autobiographies in the history of the church.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Romano-British missionary to Ireland (5th century AD); enslaved at age 16; escaped; returned as missionary bishop; planted Christianity throughout the Irish nation; left two short Latin works in his own hand (Confessio, Epistola ad Coroticum).

PATRICK, proper noun. Latin Patricius — "nobleman." From pater ("father"); the Patricii were the founding senatorial families of Rome.

Patrick of Ireland (c. 385-461 AD or c. 415-493 AD; sources differ). Romano-British Christian; captured by Irish raiders at 16; enslaved 6 years; escaped; returned as missionary bishop; established Christianity throughout Ireland.

Two authentic Latin works survive: Confessio (autobiographical defense) and Epistola ad Coroticum (excommunication of a Christian slave-raider). Feast day March 17.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 16:9-10 — "And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us. And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia."

Matthew 28:19-20 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you."

Romans 10:14-15 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent?"

Isaiah 49:6 — "I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the ends of the earth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Patrick is corrupted when his autobiographical writings are displaced by medieval shamrock-and-snake legends, when his name becomes the occasion for ethnic-pride drinking culture detached from any Christian content, or when his missionary commitment to a pagan enemy nation is treated as Irish-nationalist folklore rather than apostolic-pattern evangelism.

expand to see more

Green-beer secularization. The modern American Saint Patrick's Day — green rivers, plastic shamrocks, public drunkenness, parades sponsored by liquor brands — bears effectively no resemblance to the man it nominally commemorates. Patrick was a missionary monk who lived in poverty, traveled by foot, preached the gospel to a people who had enslaved him, and wrote two short Latin works to defend his ministry against jealous clergymen. The cultural appropriation of his name into a drinking-festival has detached him from his witness. A child named Patrick today should know it is the missionary's name, not the holiday's.

Shamrock-and-snake hagiography. The two beloved Patrick legends — that he used the shamrock to teach Trinitarian doctrine and that he banished snakes from Ireland — are medieval embellishments not present in his own writings. The Trinitarian-shamrock illustration appears no earlier than the 17th century. The snake-banishing legend is a metaphor for paganism that became literal in popular telling. The Confessio contains neither. Modern Reformed readers should honor the historical missionary the genuine sources preserve, not the medieval folklore that has accumulated around him.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin Patricius ("nobleman, member of the patrician class"), from pater ("father"). Christian use traces to Patrick of Ireland (5th c. AD).

Latin Patricius — "nobleman, of the patrician class"

From pater — "father"; the Patricii were the founding senatorial families of Rome

Christian use traces to Patrick of Ireland (5th c. AD), the Romano-British missionary to the Irish

Two authentic works survive: Confessio and Epistola ad Coroticum

Variants in modern use: Pádraig (Irish), Patrice (French), Patricio (Spanish/Italian), Patrik (Scandinavian/Slavic), Pat, Paddy, Rick

Usage

"Patrick — the Romano-British missionary to Ireland, not the drinking-holiday icon."

"Enslaved by the people he would later evangelize; his return was the most apostolic-pattern missionary action of the patristic age."

"A Reformed-friendly choice for a son: the historical Romano-British missionary whose actual Latin writings preach repentance, faith, and apostolic-pattern evangelism, not the medieval shamrock-and-snake legends or the modern green-beer holiday."
